pages.x: Pompeii was a busy town of some 11,000 people on the Bay of Naples, with temples, baths, bakeries, bars and two theatres, and rich villas along the coast. Few knew that Vesuvius, the green mountain above, was a volcano. A great earthquake in 62 had been a warning.

One day in AD 79, in late October by the newest evidence, Vesuvius blew open. A column of ash and pumice shot more than 30 km into the sky. Pliny the Younger, watching from across the bay, said it was shaped like an umbrella pine.
Pumice and ash fell on Pompeii for hours and piled up nearly three metres deep. Roofs gave way under the weight. Many people fled. Others stayed in their houses, hoping it would pass.

Pliny the Elder, admiral of the fleet at Misenum and author of a vast book about nature, sailed across the bay with warships to rescue people and see it close up. Fortune favours the brave, he said. He landed at Stabiae, and died on the beach the next morning, perhaps choked by fumes.

In the night and the next morning, avalanches of scorching gas and ash, faster than anyone could run, swept over Herculaneum and then Pompeii, killing everyone still there. Remains of some 1,150 people have been found at Pompeii so far, and over 300 by the harbour of Herculaneum.

pages.x: Years later, Pliny's nephew, Pliny the Younger, 17 at the time, wrote two letters about it for the historian Tacitus: the cloud, his uncle's death, and his own escape with his mother through a darkness like a lamp put out in a closed room. Scientists still call such eruptions Plinian.

Pompeii's walls are covered in writing: election posters, adverts for gladiator shows, lovers' notes, jokes and insults. One scribbler wondered that the wall had not fallen down under the weight of so much boring writing.

Pompeii lay buried and forgotten until digging began in 1748. In 1863 the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into hollows that bodies had left in the hardened ash, bringing back the last moments of people, and even of a dog.

The eruption froze a Roman town in a single moment: its streets, food, paintings and people. Pompeii is still being dug, millions visit it each year, and Vesuvius, which last erupted in 1944, is watched day and night.
